newsitem.title: USA: TVA reactor to be used to test tritium production.
newsitem.headline: TVA reactor to be used to test tritium production.

text.p: A Tennessee Valley Authority nuclear reactor will be used for 18 months to test whether commercial reactors will be effective producers of tritium, a radioactive gas that boosts the power of nuclear weapons, the Energy Department said Friday.

The department said it chose the TVA's Watts Bar Nuclear Plant in Spring City, Tennessee, a major electricity supplier for the Southeast, to run the test to produce about an ounce of tritium, which it said will not be used in nuclear weapons.

"This test will provide confidence to the nuclear industry and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, which regulates these plants, that making tritium in a light water reactor is technically straightforward and safe," Acting Energy Secretary Charles Curtis said in a statement.
Contract terms for the test are still being negotiated, a TVA spokeswoman said.

The Energy Department is pursuing several options to produce tritium, a relatively short-lived gas that it has not produced since 1988 and which it says it will need by 2005 to maintain the nuclear arsenal.
One involves using commercial light-water reactors such as Watts Bar, and another is to build an accelerator facility at the department's Savannah River site in South Carolina.
The department also is keeping on standby an experimental reactor at its Hanford site in Washington state that was part of the discontinued breeder reactor program and had been slated to be closed.
The department is to choose a new tritium production source next year.
With the Watts Bar test, the department said the reactor is to operate normally, but will have a few specially designed rods in four of the nearly 200 fuel assemblies in the plant's reactor core.
The special rods, which contain neither uranium nor plutonium, are designed to replace a standard component of reactor fuel assemblies, the department said.
Following the tests, the rods are to be shipped by an Energy Department carrier to its Pacific Northwest National Laboratory near the Hanford facility for examination.
Nuclear control advocates had mixed views on the test.

"We've been supportive of the concept, under very prescribed rules, to use commercial reactors to avoid having to build a dedicated production facility," Paul Leventhal, president of the Nuclear Control Institute, said.
But Leventhal said he did not believe the administration has shown there is a need to produce tritium.
